title: Workers in the vineyard (Matthew 20:1–16)
hook: those hired at the last hour get a full day's pay, and the early ones grumble

segments.voice: Yesterday, thesauros: a field's treasure, and a man who sold everything for it. Your line was in joy, not duty.

Dawn, in a village square. Men wait, hoping for a day's work. A landowner hires a crew for his vineyard, and they agree the usual wage: one silver coin, a day's pay. At nine he's back for more. At noon, more. At three, more. At five, with one hour of light left, men are still standing there. Why are you idle all day? Because no one hired us. So he sends them in too. At sunset the pay line forms, and he tells his manager: start with the last. The five o'clock crew each get one silver coin, a full day's pay for one hour. The dawn crew start doing the math. Then they get paid. One coin each.
screen: `DAWN, NINE, NOON, THREE, FIVE.` → `START WITH THE LAST.` → `ONE COIN EACH.`

segments.voice: The complaint, in the King James, is hard to argue with: "These last have wrought but one hour, and thou hast made them equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day." They have a point. It isn't fair, and the owner doesn't pretend it is. He says: friend, I did you no wrong; you agreed to a coin. Then a sharp question: "is thine eye evil, because I am good?" Why does my generosity to them feel like a loss to you? Christians read it more than one way. Some hear grace: God's welcome isn't a wage earned by the hour, and someone who comes to faith on their last day is welcomed like someone who came as a child. Others hear who belongs: old insiders and newcomers made equal. Some notice the money: one coin was the day's wage they all agreed on, so the latecomers go home with a full day's pay, like everyone else. Churches hold these readings side by side. And the English phrase the eleventh hour, for just in time, is often traced to this crew, hired at the eleventh hour of the working day. That closes a week of stories: why he told them at all, seed on every ground, a mustard seed and a pinch of yeast, a shepherd after one sheep, a woman sweeping for one coin, a treasure worth everything, and now a boss who pays the last first. In almost every one, somebody gives more than makes sense.
screen: `THEY HAVE A POINT. IT ISN'T FAIR.` · `IS THINE EYE EVIL, BECAUSE I AM GOOD?` · `GRACE, BELONGING, A FULL DAY'S PAY.` · `A WEEK OF STORIES THAT OVERPAY.` · then, large: `THE LAST SHALL BE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Think of the ledger you carry: who does the dishes, who texted last, who got the credit, who got off easy. Find one line and, without erasing it, feel what keeping it costs you. If you pray, hand it to God; if not, loosen your grip, a little.
Denarius. The silver coin, a full day's wage, that every worker goes home with, hired at dawn or at the eleventh hour.
Your line: generosity isn't fair. it's better. A week of stories, wrapped; see you on day twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians often read this parable as a picture of God's grace, given the same to people who come to faith late as to those who came early. It's a common text for sermons on envy, fairness and welcome.

original.note: Greek, from the Latin denarius: a silver coin, a laborer's day's pay. the old King James calls it a penny.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about bad management.
what it means: generosity that ignores the ledger. the owner gives the last what they need, and the first what they agreed.
what a scholar hears: the KJV's "penny" is a denarius, the day's wage they agreed on (Matthew 20:2). the last are paid first, and paid the same.

chat.says: Why did the vineyard owner pay the one-hour workers the same as everyone?
options: He chose to be generous, and no one got less than they agreed to.
He lost track of who started when, and paid everyone by mistake.
The late workers worked twice as hard to make up the time.
chat.meaning: The dawn crew got the coin they agreed to. The owner asks, "is thine eye evil, because I am good?" It's generosity, not a wage.

notes: Review 2026-10-01: cut 'most of us would sign it' (telling the listener) and 'the sharpest question'; 'many hear' to 'some hear'; the unsourced 'one coin was what a family needed to eat that day' (teach, myth, trapdoor, screen) replaced with the agreed day's wage of Matthew 20:2; 'eleventh hour comes from this story' hedged to 'is often traced to'.
Hours given in modern time (nine, noon, three, five) for the text's third, sixth, ninth and eleventh hours, counted from about 6am; confirm.
Claim that the English idiom 'at the eleventh hour' comes from this parable is widely stated; confirm.
'One coin was about what a family needed to eat that day': the denarius as a subsistence day's wage is a common scholarly estimate; confirm wording.
The reading about 'old insiders and newcomers' is kept general; some interpreters read it as Israel and the Gentiles. Stated generally to avoid any framing against Jewish listeners; confirm.
